_meta.notes: All sources are peer-reviewed or institutional. Tier A = top-tier journals (Nature, AJCN, MSSE, JISSN, etc.). Tier B = reputable institutional or good journal but lower impact. Only real URLs included.

sources.org: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
sources.reliability_notes: ISSN official position stand on creatine — gold standard reference
sources.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine (Kreider et al.)
key_claims: Creatine monohydrate 3-5g/day is safe and effective
20-40% increase in muscle PCr stores
5-15% improvement in strength
No credible evidence of kidney damage in healthy individuals

sources.reliability_notes: Seminal study by Stuart Phillips on post-exercise MPS kinetics
sources.title: Mixed muscle protein synthesis and breakdown after resistance exercise in humans (Phillips SM et al.)
key_claims: MPS elevated for 24-48 hours post-resistance exercise
MPB also elevated but to lesser degree than MPS in trained state
Net positive muscle protein balance after exercise when protein is available

sources.reliability_notes: Key pre-sleep protein study — highly cited
sources.title: Protein ingestion before sleep improves postexercise overnight recovery (Res et al.)
key_claims: 40g casein before sleep increased overnight MPS by 22%
Pre-sleep protein effectively digested and absorbed overnight
Beneficial for post-exercise recovery

sources.org: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
sources.reliability_notes: Critical review by Robert Wolfe on BCAA limitations — frequently cited
sources.title: Branched-chain amino acids and muscle protein synthesis in humans: myth or reality? (Wolfe RR)
key_claims: BCAAs cannot independently promote net muscle protein accretion
Complete EAA profile required for maximal MPS
BCAA supplementation has limited benefit when protein intake is adequate

sources.reliability_notes: Meta-analysis on protein intake for hypertrophy — consensus reference
sources.title: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults (Morton et al.)
key_claims: 1.62g protein/kg/day is the upper threshold for maximizing hypertrophy in most adults
Higher intakes (up to 2.2g/kg) may benefit some individuals
Total protein intake is the primary driver, not timing

sources.reliability_notes: Comprehensive review on sarcopenia definition and mechanisms
sources.title: Sarcopenia: current concepts (Doherty TJ)
key_claims: 1% muscle mass loss per year after age 30
3-5% per year after age 60
Sarcopenia is associated with falls, fractures, and increased mortality

sources.org: Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle
sources.reliability_notes: European Working Group revised consensus on sarcopenia definition
sources.title: Sarcopenia: revised European consensus on definition and diagnosis (Cruz-Jentoft et al.)
key_claims: Sarcopenia is now classified as a muscle disease with ICD-10 code
Low muscle strength is the primary criterion
Low muscle quantity/quality confirms diagnosis

sources.reliability_notes: Comprehensive HMB review covering all age groups
sources.title: Effects of beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate supplementation on strength and body composition across the spectrum of age (Wilson et al.)
key_claims: HMB 3g/day preserves muscle mass during catabolism
Greatest effects in elderly and untrained individuals
Inhibits ubiquitin-proteasome pathway

sources.reliability_notes: Foundational study on protein dose response for MPS — Moore et al.
sources.title: Ingested protein dose response of muscle and albumin protein synthesis after resistance exercise in young men (Moore et al.)
key_claims: 20-40g protein per meal (0.4g/kg) maximally stimulates MPS
40g marginally superior to 20g in some subjects
Excess protein above threshold is oxidized, not incorporated

sources.reliability_notes: Review on anabolic resistance in older adults
sources.title: Anabolic resistance of muscle protein turnover comes in various shapes and sizes (Burd et al.)
key_claims: Older adults exhibit anabolic resistance to protein and exercise
Higher per-meal protein doses needed in elderly
Resistance training can partially overcome anabolic resistance

sources.reliability_notes: Norton and Layman leucine threshold paper
sources.title: Leucine content of dietary proteins is a determinant of postprandial skeletal muscle protein synthesis in adult rats
key_claims: Leucine ~2-3g per meal required for maximal mTOR activation
Leucine content varies significantly across protein sources
Whey protein has highest leucine density per gram

sources.reliability_notes: Shaw et al. gelatin + Vitamin C before exercise study
sources.title: Vitamin C-enriched gelatin supplementation before intermittent activity augments collagen synthesis (Shaw et al.)
key_claims: 15g gelatin + Vitamin C 1 hour before exercise doubled collagen synthesis markers
Benefits for tendon and ligament recovery
Timing is critical: 1 hour before activity

sources.org: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
sources.reliability_notes: Schoenfeld and Aragon protein timing meta-analysis
sources.title: The effect of protein timing on muscle strength and hypertrophy: a meta-analysis (Schoenfeld & Aragon)
key_claims: Protein timing effect is minimal when total daily protein intake is equated
Post-exercise window is ~4-6 hours for practical purposes
Consuming protein at multiple times throughout the day is optimal

sources.reliability_notes: Dattilo et al. on sleep and muscle recovery — good mechanistic overview, lower journal tier
sources.title: Sleep and muscle recovery: endocrinological and molecular basis for a new and promising hypothesis (Dattilo et al.)
key_claims: 70-75% of daily GH secreted during slow-wave sleep
Sleep deprivation blunts GH pulse and impairs recovery
Adequate sleep is a prerequisite for optimal muscle adaptation
